4.1.goal: Draw 1,000 samples from a skewed population and watch the sample means form a bell-shaped sampling distribution centred on the true mean.

blocks.title: Build a population
blocks.text: A made-up population of 100,000 values, skewed to the right (a few large values), with a true mean near 30 and a true SD near 15, like the lesson's builder. The seed makes the numbers repeatable.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
population = 15 + rng.exponential(15, size=100_000)
mu = population.mean()
sigma = population.std()

print(f'population mean (mu)   = {mu:.2f}')
print(f'population SD (sigma)  = {sigma:.2f}')

blocks.title: Draw 1,000 samples of size 30
blocks.text: Each row below is one random sample of 30 people. We compute the mean of every row, so we end up with 1,000 different sample means. That pile of means is the sampling distribution.
blocks.code:
n = 30
samples = rng.choice(population, size=(1000, n))
sample_means = samples.mean(axis=1)

print('first five sample means:', sample_means[:5].round(2))
print('number of sample means:', len(sample_means))

blocks.title: Centre and spread
blocks.text: The sample means should centre on mu, and their spread (the standard error) should be close to sigma divided by the square root of n.
blocks.code:
print(f'mean of the sample means = {sample_means.mean():.2f}  (mu = {mu:.2f})')
print(f'SD of the sample means    = {sample_means.std(ddof=1):.2f}')
print(f'theory sigma / sqrt(n)    = {sigma / np.sqrt(n):.2f}')

blocks.title: Draw the sampling distribution
blocks.text: A histogram shows the shape. Even though the population is skewed, the sample means pile up in a fairly symmetric bell around mu. The dashed line marks mu.
blocks.code:
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.4))
plt.hist(sample_means, bins=30, color='steelblue', edgecolor='white')
plt.axvline(mu, color='black', linestyle='--', label='population mean')
plt.xlabel('sample mean (n = 30)')
plt.ylabel('number of samples')
plt.title('Sampling distribution of the mean')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

r.code:
set.seed(42)
population <- 15 + rexp(100000, rate = 1/15)
means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(population, 30, replace = TRUE)))
mean(population)
mean(means)
sd(means)
15 / sqrt(30)
hist(means, breaks = 30)
r.expect: mean(population) about 30.05; mean(means) about 30; sd(means) about 2.8; 15 / sqrt(30) = 2.738 (Python: 30.05, 29.99, 2.83, 2.75)
r.note: Random draws differ between R and Python, so simulated numbers are close but not identical; the theory value 15 / sqrt(30) = 2.74 is exact.

spss.menu: Transform > Compute Variable (with Random Number Functions), then Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives
spss.syntax:
SET SEED=42.
INPUT PROGRAM.
LOOP s = 1 TO 1000.
COMPUTE total = 0.
LOOP i = 1 TO 30.
COMPUTE total = total + 15 + RV.EXP(1/15).
END LOOP.
COMPUTE xbar = total/30.
END CASE.
END LOOP.
END FILE.
END INPUT PROGRAM.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=xbar /STATISTICS=MEAN STDDEV.
spss.note: This draws each sample straight from the skewed model instead of a stored population, so the mean of xbar is near 30 and its SD near 2.7, close to but not exactly the Python numbers.

stata.code:
clear
set seed 42
set obs 1000
generate xbar = 0
forvalues i = 1/30 {
    quietly replace xbar = xbar + (15 + rexponential(15)) / 30
}
summarize xbar
display 15 / sqrt(30)
histogram xbar
stata.note: Each of the 1,000 rows gets the mean of 30 fresh draws; the Mean and Std. dev. of xbar should be near 30 and 2.7, close to but not identical to Python.

4.2.goal: Compute the standard error of a mean by formula, then check it against simulated sample means and watch it shrink as n grows.

blocks.title: SE by formula
blocks.text: The lesson's eight midterm scores. The standard error is the sample SD (ddof=1) divided by the square root of n. It says how precisely this class mean is pinned down.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([72, 85, 68, 91, 77, 83, 64, 80])
n = len(scores)
mean = scores.mean()
s = scores.std(ddof=1)
se = s / np.sqrt(n)

print(f'mean = {mean:.2f}')
print(f's    = {s:.2f}')
print(f'SE   = {se:.2f}')

blocks.title: A population to test it on
blocks.text: To check the formula we need many samples, so we build a skewed population (true mean 30, true SD 15) and draw a lot of samples from it.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
population = 15 + rng.exponential(15, size=100_000)
sigma = population.std()
print(f'population SD = {sigma:.2f}')

blocks.title: SE shrinks as n grows
blocks.text: For each n we draw 2,000 samples and take the SD of their means. That should match sigma / sqrt(n), and also the SE we would get from a single sample. Each time n is multiplied by 4, the SE halves.
blocks.code:
print('   n   SD of 2000 means   sigma/sqrt(n)   s/sqrt(n), one sample')
for n in (10, 40, 160, 640):
    means = rng.choice(population, size=(2000, n)).mean(axis=1)
    one = rng.choice(population, size=n)
    print(f'{n:4d}   {means.std(ddof=1):14.2f}   {sigma / np.sqrt(n):13.2f}   {one.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n):12.2f}')

blocks.title: Plan a sample size
blocks.text: To get an SE of 1 when sigma is about 15, solve 15 / sqrt(n) = 1. Always round the answer up.
blocks.code:
target_se = 1
sigma_guess = 15
n_needed = int(np.ceil((sigma_guess / target_se) ** 2))
print('sample size needed:', n_needed)

r.code:
scores <- c(72, 85, 68, 91, 77, 83, 64, 80)
mean(scores)
sd(scores)
sd(scores) / sqrt(length(scores))
set.seed(7)
for (n in c(10, 40, 160, 640)) print(sd(replicate(2000, mean(15 + rexp(n, 1/15)))))
r.expect: mean 77.5; sd 9.087; standard error 3.213; then four simulated SDs near 4.7, 2.35, 1.18 and 0.59 (Python: 4.79, 2.36, 1.20, 0.57)
r.note: sd() already uses n - 1, like ddof=1. The simulated SDs are close to, not identical to, Python's; the formula SE of 3.21 is exact.

4.3.goal: Show that sample means from a very skewed population become more symmetric and bell-shaped as the sample size grows from 1 to 5 to 30.

blocks.title: A skewed population
blocks.text: Waiting times in a clinic: exponential, with a mean of 10 minutes and an SD of 10. Lots of short waits and a long tail of rare long ones, so it is clearly skewed to the right.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(99)

def sample_means(n, reps=5000):
    return rng.exponential(10, size=(reps, n)).mean(axis=1)

single = rng.exponential(10, size=5000)
print(f'skewness of single waits = {stats.skew(single):.2f}')

blocks.title: Skewness of the sample means
blocks.text: Skewness is 0 for a perfectly symmetric shape. For each n we take 5,000 sample means and measure their skewness. It falls towards 0 roughly like 2 divided by the square root of n.
blocks.code:
print('  n   skewness of means   2/sqrt(n)')
for n in (1, 5, 30):
    m = sample_means(n)
    print(f'{n:3d}   {stats.skew(m):15.2f}   {2 / np.sqrt(n):9.2f}')

blocks.title: Three histograms
blocks.text: The same story as a picture. With n = 1 we see the skewed population itself. With n = 5 the shape is already more balanced, and with n = 30 it looks close to a bell.
blocks.code:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6, 3.4), sharex=True)
for ax, n in zip(axes, (1, 5, 30)):
    ax.hist(sample_means(n), bins=np.linspace(0, 40, 41), color='steelblue', edgecolor='white')
    ax.set_title(f'n = {n}')
    ax.set_yticks([])
axes[1].set_xlabel('sample mean (minutes)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

blocks.title: Use the bell curve
blocks.text: The lesson's clinic question: for n = 40 patients, how often does the mean wait reach 12 minutes or more? The CLT lets us use a normal curve with mean 10 and SE = 10 divided by the square root of 40.
blocks.code:
se = 10 / np.sqrt(40)
p_clt = stats.norm.sf(12, loc=10, scale=se)
simulated = (sample_means(40, reps=20000) >= 12).mean()

print(f'SE = {se:.3f}')
print(f'CLT answer       P(mean >= 12) = {p_clt:.3f}')
print(f'simulation (20k) P(mean >= 12) = {simulated:.3f}')

r.code:
skew <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / mean((x - mean(x))^2)^1.5
set.seed(99)
for (n in c(1, 5, 30)) print(skew(replicate(5000, mean(rexp(n, rate = 1/10)))))
pnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = 10 / sqrt(40), lower.tail = FALSE)
r.expect: skewness about 1.9, 0.9, 0.35 for n = 1, 5, 30 (Python: 1.93, 0.85, 0.33); pnorm answer 0.1029
r.note: Base R has no skewness function, so we write the same formula SciPy uses. Simulated skewness values are close to Python's, not identical; the pnorm answer is exact.

spss.menu: Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives > Options > Skewness
spss.syntax:
SET SEED=99.
INPUT PROGRAM.
LOOP s = 1 TO 5000.
COMPUTE x1 = RV.EXP(1/10).
COMPUTE total = 0.
LOOP i = 1 TO 30.
COMPUTE total = total + RV.EXP(1/10).
END LOOP.
COMPUTE mean30 = total/30.
END CASE.
END LOOP.
END FILE.
END INPUT PROGRAM.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=x1 mean30 /STATISTICS=MEAN STDDEV SKEWNESS.
spss.note: x1 is a single wait (n = 1) and mean30 is a mean of 30 waits, so you can compare their skewness. SPSS uses a slightly adjusted skewness formula and its own random numbers, so values are close to Python's, not identical.

stata.code:
clear
set seed 99
set obs 5000
generate x1 = rexponential(10)
generate mean30 = 0
forvalues i = 1/30 {
    quietly replace mean30 = mean30 + rexponential(10) / 30
}
tabstat x1 mean30, statistics(mean sd skewness)
display 1 - normal((12 - 10) / (10 / sqrt(40)))
stata.note: Stata's skewness uses the same formula as SciPy. Simulated values are close to Python's but not identical; the last line gives the exact normal answer of 0.103.

4.4.goal: Simulate thousands of polls to see that the spread of the sample proportion matches the formula square root of p(1-p)/n.

blocks.title: One poll
blocks.text: The lesson's poll: the true support for a bill is p = 0.54 and we ask n = 1,500 voters. Each voter says yes with probability p, so the number of yes answers is a binomial draw.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)
p, n = 0.54, 1500

yes = rng.binomial(n, p)
print(f'yes answers: {yes} of {n}')
print(f'sample proportion p-hat = {yes / n:.4f}')

blocks.title: Ten thousand polls
blocks.text: Now run the same poll 10,000 times. Each p-hat differs a little because of sampling variability. Their average should be near p, and their SD should be near the formula.
blocks.code:
p_hats = rng.binomial(n, p, size=10_000) / n

print(f'mean of p-hats          = {p_hats.mean():.4f}')
print(f'SD of p-hats            = {p_hats.std(ddof=1):.4f}')
print(f'sqrt(p(1-p)/n) formula  = {np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n):.4f}')

blocks.title: Small samples wobble more
blocks.text: The lesson's three cases. The last column checks the rule that n times p and n times (1 minus p) should both be at least 10 for the normal model to fit well.
blocks.code:
print('   n     p   SD of p-hats   formula   both n*p, n*(1-p) >= 10?')
for n, p in ((20, 0.35), (200, 0.40), (1500, 0.54)):
    ph = rng.binomial(n, p, size=10_000) / n
    ok = n * p >= 10 and n * (1 - p) >= 10
    print(f'{n:5d}  {p:.2f}   {ph.std(ddof=1):11.4f}   {np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n):7.4f}   {ok}')

blocks.title: The margin of error
blocks.text: A 95% margin of error is about 1.96 standard errors. If that is right, about 95% of polls should land within that distance of the true p.
blocks.code:
n, p = 1500, 0.54
moe = 1.96 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
p_hats = rng.binomial(n, p, size=10_000) / n
inside = (np.abs(p_hats - p) <= moe).mean()

print(f'margin of error = {moe:.4f}')
print(f'share of polls within it = {inside:.3f}')

r.code:
set.seed(2024)
p <- 0.54; n <- 1500
p_hats <- rbinom(10000, n, p) / n
mean(p_hats)
sd(p_hats)
sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
r.note: rbinom(10000, n, p) draws 10,000 polls at once. Simulated values are close to Python's but not identical; the formula value 0.0129 is exact.

4.5.goal: Bootstrap one small sample of five heart rates: get a standard error and a 95% interval without any formula, then compare with the t-interval.

blocks.title: The sample
blocks.text: Five resting heart rates (bpm) from the lesson. The classic formula SE = s / sqrt(n) is our benchmark.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

data = np.array([62, 70, 68, 75, 65])
n = len(data)
se = data.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)

print(f'mean = {data.mean():.1f}')
print(f's    = {data.std(ddof=1):.2f}')
print(f'classic SE = {se:.2f}')

blocks.title: Resample 5,000 times
blocks.text: Each resample draws 5 values from our data with replacement (the same person can appear twice), then takes the mean. We keep all 5,000 means.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(2025)
resamples = rng.choice(data, size=(5000, n), replace=True)
boot_means = resamples.mean(axis=1)

print('one resample:', resamples[0], ' mean =', resamples[0].mean())
print(f'average of boot means = {boot_means.mean():.2f}')

blocks.title: Bootstrap SE and interval
blocks.text: The SD of the bootstrap means is the bootstrap standard error. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the means form a 95% percentile interval.
blocks.code:
boot_se = boot_means.std(ddof=1)
low, high = np.percentile(boot_means, [2.5, 97.5])

print(f'bootstrap SE = {boot_se:.2f}')
print(f'95% percentile interval = ({low:.1f}, {high:.1f})')

blocks.title: Compare with the t-interval
blocks.text: With only five values the t-interval has to be wide to be honest. The bootstrap interval is narrower, because resampling cannot invent information a tiny sample does not contain.
blocks.code:
t_low, t_high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n - 1, loc=data.mean(), scale=se)

print(f't-interval        = ({t_low:.1f}, {t_high:.1f})')
print(f'bootstrap interval = ({low:.1f}, {high:.1f})')
print(f'widths: t = {t_high - t_low:.1f}, bootstrap = {high - low:.1f}')

r.code:
hr <- c(62, 70, 68, 75, 65)
set.seed(2025)
boot_means <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(hr, replace = TRUE)))
sd(boot_means)
quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
t.test(hr)$conf.int
r.expect: bootstrap sd about 1.99; 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles about 64.4 and 72; t.test conf.int 61.85 to 74.15 (Python: 1.99, (64.4, 72.0), (61.9, 74.1))
r.note: sample(hr, replace = TRUE) draws a resample of the same size. Bootstrap numbers are close to Python's but not identical; the t-interval is exact.

spss.menu: Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Explore, then press the Bootstrap button and tick Perform bootstrapping (Number of samples 5000, Percentile)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / hr.
BEGIN DATA
62 70 68 75 65
END DATA.
BOOTSTRAP
  /SAMPLING METHOD=SIMPLE
  /VARIABLES INPUT=hr
  /CRITERIA CILEVEL=95 CITYPE=PERCENTILE NSAMPLES=5000
  /MISSING USER=EXCLUDE.
EXAMINE VARIABLES=hr
  /PLOT=NONE
  /STATISTICS=DESCRIPTIVES.
spss.note: The Bootstrap button appears on many dialogs. In the output, the Bootstrap table gives the bias, Std. Error and 95% percentile interval for the mean; the ordinary Descriptives table gives the t-interval. Results are close to Python's, not identical.

input hr
62
70
68
75
65
end

estat bootstrap, percentile
ci means hr
stata.note: estat bootstrap, percentile shows the bootstrap SE and the percentile interval; ci means gives the t-interval. Bootstrap results are close to Python's, not identical.
